Guys, this is the most honest analysis I've felt regarding how people talk and what it actually means.  

People who speak softly are often labeled as manipulative and cunning. But people who speak loudly are labeled as rude and tactless.  

That's a judgment that needs to be questioned.  

If tone of voice truly reflected character, we should be able to see a consistent pattern. Not just judging from one context.

Here are the facts.  

People who speak softly aren't automatically backstabbers. Many doctors, teachers, and counselors speak softly — precisely because they are trained to make others feel safe and heard.  

People who speak loudly aren't automatically honest. Many high-level scammers actually speak with full confidence and high volume — because manufactured confidence indeed sounds loud.  

People who speak fast aren't always smart. Sometimes they're just nervous, or afraid of silence because silence feels like losing control.  

This isn't about character. This is about context and habits formed by the environment.  

"Read personality from how they talk" content is mostly just neatly packaged generalizations.

And the ones who believe it most easily are us — who really want a simple way to instantly read others without needing much time.  

And for our daily relationships, this is directly relevant.  

We aren't psychologists. But we often act as if one trait is enough to judge someone completely.  

Our relationships become shallow. Our prejudices get stronger. And part of that isn't because the person is actually like that — but because we judge too quickly before truly getting to know them.

Guys, this is a story that I think is both funny and revealing about how [LOCATION] people view [LOCATION].  

Nikita Bier — the Head of Product at X/Twitter, whose life revolves around growth and user behavior — found an anomaly on his platform. 

One entity. 30 active accounts. All from Indonesian IP addresses. 

The pattern was too consistent, too organized to be done manually.  

He immediately went into investigation mode. His initial assumption made total sense from a tech founder's perspective: this must be a bot farm. There must be a sophisticated automation tool. Maybe an AI script that can simulate human behavior very convincingly. 

He was genuinely curious — what technology could allow one entity to operate 30 accounts at once without getting caught?  

So he did a deep analysis. He looked for the tool's fingerprint. He investigated the behavior patterns one by one. The result wasn't what he expected.  

Not AI.
Not a bot.
Not any kind of automation tool.
[ORGANIZATION] aku takut akan kehilangan [ORGANIZATION] wait, sorry. Typing this prompt while listening to [PERSON]. 

Hold on. Let's restart. Not enough AI. 

Not AI.
Not a bot.
Not any kind of automation tool.
[ORGANIZATION] aku takut akan kehilangan [ORGANIZATION], sorry. Typing this prompt while listening to [PERSON].

There.

Actually, well... it was just the person being a multitasker. One Indonesian human, with patience and full dedication, operating those 30 accounts manually. Tab by tab. Account by account. No fancy scripts, no AI models behind it. Just pure effort that was so incredibly consistent that the pattern looked like a machine. 

And this is what's interesting.  

Nikita Bier — who is surrounded by AI tools, automation, and high-tech every day — couldn't imagine that there was a human willing and able to do that manually. His default assumption went straight to technology, not the human. 

Because in his world, nobody wants to put in that much effort if there's a tool that can handle it.  

But it's different here.  

We grew up in an ecosystem where resourcefulness isn't an option, it's a survival skill. Where if the tool doesn't exist, you do it yourself. Where consistency and volume aren't about machine capacity, but about how willing you are to sit down and do it one by one.  

Nikita Bier thought he found the technology of the future.

What he found: we are the real artificial intelligence. AI = Actual Indonesian. LOL. 😅

Guys I just realized something that's been hiding in plain sight but turns out its origins are way different from what we think now.
I thought [PERSON] was made from the start to be the biggest video platform.
And turns out that wasn't the initial goal.
YouTube was originally created by [PERSON], [PERSON], and [PERSON] with an idea that was much simpler than what people imagine today.
A concept that didn't even have anything to do with video sharing as we know it today.
Stop for a second and understand what that means.
All this time the general narrative has been that [ORGANIZATION] was designed from the start to be a place for people to upload any video and naturally grew into the global platform we use every day now.

That's an assumption that's just been taken for granted by many people for a long time.
But the reality is the original idea was a video dating platform to introduce yourself.
And that concept didn't work.
At all.

The platform was supposed to be filled with videos introducing yourself, your interests, and what you're looking for in a partner—like a modern dating profile based on personal videos to attract other users on the internet.
And they even tried to push users to upload that kind of content, especially women, but almost no one was interested in using the platform for that purpose.
This wasn't just a small product failure.
This was a failure of the core concept that was the initial foundation of the platform before it pivoted into something much bigger than the founders' original plan.
And this context explains why that change of direction happened.

Why the platform didn't grow according to the original plan.
Why users actually used the platform in a different way than expected.

This isn't just a story about a product that failed at the start.
It's about how user behavior can change the direction of a platform.
And create something much bigger than the original idea.
And what finally changed everything was the way users started using the platform.
They started uploading random videos, personal moments, and funny content without following the dating concept designed from the start.

One shift in behavior that immediately opened a new direction.
Everything grew in a direction that wasn't planned before.
A platform that originally had a narrow goal turned into a global video-sharing hub.
Everyone started seeing new potential from the freedom of uploading content.
And all of that shaped YouTube into what's known by the whole world today.
Everyone finally realized that the true value wasn't in the initial idea, but in how the users actually used it.
